title: Lead sheets versus written arrangements in the Waller group
summary: A lead sheet was enough for melodic work; written arrangements were needed only for many instruments moving together.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When -- when you were working out a piece, or the various things that you played, were they all just head -- head arrangements, ad lib, or did you work things out?

No, well we had -- all you need's a lead sheet, on anything. I mean what's happening, what's going down, and a good musician, even today, I mean on anything, give him a lead -- unless it's a lot of things happening, changing from here to there, a zzz, zzz, zzz together, eight or ten or fifteen instruments, doing it together, then you've got to have it on paper. Okay.

But if it's a matter that -- a matter of melody, or something, you don't need, and then you've got to have an arrangement so you can end up where those guys end up. You know. That's the arrangement. And --
Well once -- let's say once you've made a record of something, then did you sort of try and stick to the record, or --
